title: The Letter to the Romans
lead: Romans is the longest and most influential of Paul's letters. Written from Corinth in about AD 56–57 to the house churches of Rome, a city Paul had not yet visited, it sets out the good news as God's righteousness for Jew and Gentile alike: the world's guilt (1:18–3:20), righteousness through faith (3:21–4:25), life in Christ and the Spirit (5–8), the place of Israel (9–11), and the shape of the Christian life (12:1–15:13). It shaped Augustine, Luther, Wesley and Barth, and the debates about justification, original sin, election, Israel and the state all return to it.

sections.b: Paul greets the Romans and states his theme (1:1–17). He then shows that Gentiles and Jews alike are under sin (1:18–3:20) and that God's righteousness has been made plain in Christ for all who believe (3:21–4:25). Chapters 5–8 describe the life that results: peace, freedom from sin and the law, the Spirit, adoption and hope. Chapters 9–11 ask what has become of Israel. Chapters 12–15 turn to how believers are to live together, and chapter 16 greets named friends.
sections.refs: Romans 1:16–17; Romans 3:21–26; Romans 5:1–11; Romans 8:1–39; Romans 9:1–11:36; Romans 12:1–15:13; Romans 16:1–27

sections.b: Scholars debate the purpose: a summary of the gospel as Paul's last will and testament, a base for his mission to Spain, a plea for unity between Jewish and Gentile believers after the edict of Claudius, or a rehearsal of his defense before going to Jerusalem. Most hold that several of these overlap. The question is called the Romans debate.

sections.h: Romans in the history of the church
sections.b: Augustine's conversion in a Milan garden (about AD 386) came as he read Romans 13:13–14. Pelagius and Augustine fought over 5:12 and 7. Luther's discovery that "the righteousness of God" (1:17) is a gift began the Reformation; John Wesley's heart was "strangely warmed" at Aldersgate in 1738 as Luther's preface to Romans was read; Karl Barth's commentary of 1919 shook liberal theology. Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant readings still differ on justification, sin and election.
